request.content:
Every morning starts the same way in our house. The kettle goes on before anyone speaks, the curtains open, and the cat waits by the door as if it has been there all night. It is a small ritual, but it sets the pace for everything that follows.

The first habit is simple: drink a glass of water before your coffee. After a night of sleep, your body is a little dry, and that glass wakes you up more gently than any alarm. Keep the glass by the sink, so you see it, and you will not forget it.

The second habit is a short walk. Ten minutes is enough. Walk to the corner shop, around the block, or just up and down the garden. You will notice the light, the sounds of the street, and the people who are already on their way to work. By the time you come back, your head is clearer, and the day ahead feels possible.

The third habit is the hardest, because it asks you to do nothing at all. Before you open your phone, sit for two minutes and think about the one thing that matters most today. Not the ten things on your list, just one. Write it on a piece of paper if it helps. When the day gets busy, and it will, that one thing is the line you come back to.

None of these habits is new, and none of them costs anything. What makes them work is doing them every day, in the same order, until they stop feeling like a plan and start feeling like the way your mornings simply are. Try them for a week, and see how your evenings change too.

request.content:
كل يوم الصبح بيبدأ بنفس الطريقة في بيتنا. البراد بيتحط على النار قبل ما حد يتكلم، والستاير بتتفتح، والقطة بتستنى جنب الباب كأنها قاعدة هناك طول الليل. دي حاجة صغيرة، بس هي اللي بتحدد إيقاع اليوم كله.

أول عادة سهلة جداً: اشرب كوباية مية قبل القهوة. بعد النوم جسمك بيبقى ناشف شوية، والكوباية دي بتصحيك بهدوء أكتر من أي منبه. سيب الكوباية جنب الحوض عشان تشوفها، وساعتها مش هتنساها أبداً.

تاني عادة هي مشوار قصير. عشر دقايق كفاية. امشي لحد المحل اللي على الناصية، أو لف حوالين البيت، أو حتى اتمشى في الجنينة. هتاخد بالك من النور، ومن أصوات الشارع، ومن الناس اللي نازلة شغلها بدري. ولما ترجع، دماغك هتبقى أصفى، واليوم اللي جاي هيبان أسهل.

تالت عادة هي الأصعب، عشان مطلوب منك فيها إنك متعملش أي حاجة. قبل ما تفتح الموبايل، اقعد دقيقتين وفكر في أهم حاجة لازم تحصل النهارده. مش عشر حاجات، حاجة واحدة بس. اكتبها في ورقة لو ده هيساعدك. ولما اليوم يزحم، وهو أكيد هيزحم، الحاجة دي هي اللي ترجعلها.

ولا عادة من دول جديدة، ولا واحدة فيهم بتكلف أي فلوس. اللي بيخليهم ينفعوا إنك تعملهم كل يوم بنفس الترتيب، لحد ما يبطلوا يبقوا خطة ويبقوا ببساطة شكل الصبح بتاعك. جربهم أسبوع، وشوف المسا بتاعك هيتغير إزاي.

request.content:
The harbour wakes up long before the town does. By five, the first boats are already coming in, low in the water, and the gulls follow them in wide, lazy circles. The fishermen do not talk much at that hour. They tie up, lift the crates onto the stone, and wave to the buyers who have been waiting by the wall with their flasks of tea.

By six the market is open. It is not a large market, a single row of tables under a long white awning, but everything on it was in the sea a few hours ago. There are sardines laid out in silver rows, a few proud sea bass, a tray of small red mullet, and in a bucket at the end, a pile of crabs that will not stay still. The prices are written in chalk on little boards, and they change as the morning goes on.

Maria has had the third table for twenty-two years. She learned the trade from her father, who learned it from his, and she can tell where a fish was caught by the colour of its eyes. Regulars come to her not only for the fish but for the advice: how long to grill it, which herbs to use, whether today is a day for soup or for something simple with lemon and salt. She never writes anything down. She simply remembers who likes what, and puts it aside before they ask.

Around eight, the town arrives. Parents on the way to school stop for something for dinner, cooks from the restaurants on the square come with their lists, and a few visitors take photographs of the crabs, which do not seem to mind. The noise rises, the awning fills with voices, and for an hour the harbour is the busiest place for miles.

Then, almost as quickly as it began, it is over. By ten the tables are washed down, the boards are wiped clean, and the boats rock quietly at their moorings. The fishermen go home to sleep, and the gulls settle on the wall to wait for tomorrow. Maria counts her takings, folds her apron, and walks up the hill for a late breakfast of bread, olives and very strong coffee.

In winter the market changes. The storms keep the smaller boats in, the awning comes down, and the tables move into the old net store by the slipway. There is less to sell and more time to talk, and the same few faces come every day, as much for the company as for the fish. Maria brings a radio and a heater, and on the coldest mornings somebody always arrives with a tin of warm pastries to share.

People sometimes ask her whether she ever wanted a different life, somewhere bigger, with regular hours and a roof that does not flap in the wind. She always laughs at that. Where else, she says, would I see the sun come up over the water every morning, and know the name of everyone who buys my fish? Some jobs you choose, and some jobs choose you. This one, she says, chose well.
